Unified execution profiles and resource barriers (execution_profiles.py, M5-P3-02) enforce shared/exclusive barriers and capacity slots within a single application process (matching worker leases, task events, and model admission); static shell/AST inspection cannot decide arbitrary Turing-complete obfuscation pre-execution when container isolation is unqualified, relying on post-execution quarantine/uncertain marking until M5-P3-01 live container qualification passes.

Harness task-event store (task_events.py, M5-P1-07) and workspace snapshot store (workspace_snapshots.py, M5-P2-01) assume a single application process per session, matching the worker-lease model; cross-process concurrent appends are unsupported and not claimed safe.

The edit ledger and observed-version index assume one application process per session (same assumption as the durable event stream and worker leases); a second process editing the same workspace is not detected. The .harnesses/edits directory is bounded per session (4 MiB rotation) but has no cross-session pruning (M5-P2-02).

The M5-P2-03 rollback journal stores both the pre- and post-edit bytes of every managed edit in the edit CAS (.harnesses/edits/blobs) and has no garbage collection; the store grows with edit volume until a retention story adds pruning. Rollback covers managed edits only, and its line-based merge refuses rather than guesses on a user edit inside a region the batch wrote.

M5-P3-02 review (post-merge, independent session): docs/execution-profiles.md claimed 'recursive inspection of inline sh -c / bash -c' payloads, but the code only handled python -c, so a quoted payload token (sh -c 'cat .env', bash -c 'echo x > .git/hooks/pre-commit', perl/node/ruby -e '<path>') was allowed where the same command written directly was refused. Fixed in the reviewing session's PR by re-parsing shell -c payloads (bounded to three levels), refusing a shell that reads its command from stdin, and checking the path tokens of perl/ruby/node/php/lua inline code; the remaining limits of pre-execution text inspection (script file contents, runtime-built paths, encoded payloads) are now stated in docs/execution-profiles.md instead of being implied away. The sandbox (M5-P3-01) remains the boundary for those, which is another reason unqualified isolation keeps host execution unavailable.

M5-P3-02 review, second finding: the post-execution reconciliation layer judged a newly created .git/config 'benign' using a regex over raw text, but git writes the sectioned form ([credential]\n helper = ...), so credential.helper (and filter.*.clean|smudge, include.path, includeIf) went undetected and the run reported clean instead of policy_violation -- no quarantine, no uncertainty, follow-up actions not blocked. Post-execution detection was weaker than the pre-execution rule that refuses the same directives. Fixed by parsing sections/subsections/keys and resolving each directive to its dotted name; a plain git-init-shaped config still passes. The less general point: two layers that enforce the same policy must share the predicate rather than each writing their own matcher.

Process supervision and containment (process_supervision.py, M5-P3-03, ADR-0013) tracks process groups, ppid descendants, and M5_SUPERVISION_ID detached trees within a single Studio process; in STUDIO_EXECUTION_MODE=host a deliberately adversarial child that scrubs M5_SUPERVISION_ID and double-forks before tree enumeration cannot be kernel-guaranteed without OS cgroups/PID namespaces (M5-P3-01).

M5-P3-02 review, third pass (on the first fix's own code): the inline-payload inspection added in PR #62 still had two holes, found by re-testing it adversarially. (a) The wrapper skip consumed only tokens starting with '-', so for wrappers whose option takes a separate value the option's VALUE was read as the executable: `env -u HOME sh -c 'cat .env'`, `nice -n 5 sh -c ...`, `time -f %s sh -c ...` all skipped the shell entirely. (b) The inline-code path scan matched only paths containing a separator, so a bare secret name in interpreter code (`node --eval 'require("fs").readFileSync(".env")'`, `perl -e'open(F,".env")'`) was invisible. Fixed by resolving wrapper options with their values (_ep_skip_wrapper), accepting the glued `-e<payload>` form, matching bare dotted names, and refusing a shell asked to read its command from stdin (`-s`). The lesson generalises: a fix for a security boundary needs the same adversarial pass as the code it replaced.

M5-P3-02 review, fourth pass: the `.git/config` fix (#63) judged configuration as a FILE, but git accepts the same directives in-band. `git -c include.path=/tmp/evil.cfg status` was allowed: the command-line guard was a regex over the raw text, so it missed `include.path` entirely, and shell quoting (`git -c core."fs"monitor=...`) defeats text matching even for the keys it did list. `-c`, glued `-ckey=value`, `--config-env`, `git config key value` and `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>`/`GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` are now judged from parsed tokens against one shared predicate (_ep_git_config_key_is_dangerous) used by both the file parser and the command scanner, so the two cannot drift again. Same lesson as the previous pass: a security fix has to cover every way the underlying tool accepts the setting, not just the way the report named.

decisions: An edit is a compare-and-swap on content, not a path: the expectation is resolved from (1) the caller's expected_sha256, (2) the version read_file handed this session, (3) the bytes this runtime last wrote, and refused on mismatch. A target that was never read and never written is still a first write, so create-then-edit flows keep working.

The expectation is re-checked immediately before the rename through the same directory descriptor (hash_confined_child), because a check that happens only before the write is exactly the read-then-write race the story exists to close.

read_file hashes the bytes on disk rather than the decoded text, so the digest the agent quotes back as expected_sha256 is the digest the writer compares (no locale/encoding drift between read and write).

The edit ledger is an append-only per-session JSONL under the harness store (O_APPEND + fsync, bounded by rotation) rather than a schema-v4 SQLite table: it is per-session, append-only and bounded, and putting the edit history inside the exported database would duplicate user file metadata there.

Observed versions are durable (atomic JSON index, bounded to 2048 entries) because the agent's transcript survives a restart; downgrading 'I read version X' to 'no expectation' after a restart would silently weaken the guarantee.

Path refusals are structured (`unauthorized_path`/`unsafe_path`) instead of surfacing as a generic tool error, and symlinks are refused even when they point inside the workspace: a managed edit edits the file the caller named or nothing.

A ledger append failure after the bytes are on disk cannot un-write them, so the edit reports edit_transaction=null plus an edit/ledger_failed event rather than claiming a rollback it did not perform.

decisions: Rollback is a durable per-batch journal plus a version-checked inverse patch, never `git reset --hard` / `git checkout -- PATH` / `git stash`: the destructive forms discard the user's uncommitted work and cannot be scoped to a runtime batch without assuming a clean tree at a known commit (ADR-0007).

The journal records the intended step BEFORE the write. The planner decides from bytes on disk, so a step whose write never happened plans as already_reverted (no-op) and a step whose write did happen restores the stored pre-image; recording after the write would lose exactly the step an interrupted run needs.

A refused plan performs no writes at all, including for the individually safe paths: best-effort partial rollback would leave a third state that is neither before nor after, with no record of it. The batch is persisted as unresolved with per-path reasons plus a dry-run plan.

Three-way merge with `post` as the common base is used when the file changed after the batch: hunks that turn post back into pre are applied onto the current text and disjoint user edits survive; a collision with a user edit is a conflict rather than a guess.

The reconciliation gate blocks only on in_flight/uncertain managed-edit actions (write_file/edit_file), because those are the writes rollback could race and its own restores are compare-and-swapped; other tools' unresolved actions are reported as warnings. An unreadable ledger blocks the rollback (fail closed).
Acknowledgement of unresolved actions is an explicit caller decision (acknowledge_unresolved) recorded in the batch notes and the edit/rollback task event, so a silent override cannot happen.

Batch documents are atomic JSON files rather than a new SQLite table: they are small, written and read whole, need no schema migration, and keep the edit history out of the exported database (same reasoning as ADR-0006's edit ledger).
Private module globals in edit_rollback are prefixed _erb_* because the standalone bundle concatenates inlined modules into one namespace; the collision guard test pins that property.

evidence: Deliverable (tooling, not a result): scripts/qualify_environment.py --sandbox executes the sandbox suite through app._execute_limited with STUDIO_EXECUTION_MODE=sandbox and a hardened `--network=none --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges --pull=never` container built by container_argv; tests/test_qualify_environment.py::test_container_argv_matches_the_product_hardening_flags asserts the suite's flags stay equal to app._sandbox_command's (single bind mount, no --privileged).

Adversarial matrix observed in one container run: /etc/hostname via /etc, /workspace/../etc and /proc/1/root/etc, a workspace symlink pointing at a host file, a direct TCP connect to 1.1.1.1:443, an inherited STUDIO_QUALIFICATION_SENTINEL environment value, and a raw AF_INET socket are each required to fail; any leak makes the check fail and the suite unqualified (tests: test_sandbox_suite_fails_when_an_escape_is_observed).

Resource and lifecycle limits: 3 GiB allocation under --memory 512m must die (exit 137 or MemoryError), and a background `sleep 300` descendant must leave no container behind (`docker ps --filter name=`). Positive compatibility: code runs and its write lands in the mounted workspace.

No silent host fallback: p3.product.no_host_fallback points STUDIO_SANDBOX_RUNTIME at a nonexistent binary (must deny) and then runs the real configuration (no host marker file may appear); a simulated host execution is reported as a failure (test_sandbox_suite_reports_host_execution_as_a_failure). scripts/isolation_smoke.py --live is executed as one aggregated check.

Blocker unchanged: no container runtime exists in this evidence environment (docker/podman not on PATH). The live run therefore reports M5-P3-01 as blocked, with every container probe recorded skip and the reason; no isolation guarantee is claimed. Evidence: scripts/qualify_environment.py --all locally exits 2 with `M5-P3-01: blocked`.

Next action: the owner runs `python3 scripts/qualify_environment.py --sandbox --json <path> --markdown <path>` (or ./scripts/qualify_environment.sh) on the Docker host; only a `qualified` record may move this story off blocked (docs/qualification-suite.md).

First-run hardening of the qualification tooling (so the owner's run cannot report a false verdict): --dry-run prints every command without executing any of them (tests: test_dry_run_prints_the_plan_and_touches_nothing, test_dry_run_is_explicit_about_skipped_measurements); a missing image is now blocked/exit 2 instead of unqualified, because nothing about isolation was observed (test_a_missing_image_blocks_the_suite_instead_of_accusing_isolation, test_a_runtime_without_the_image_never_produces_a_pass); the positive probe reports what the container sees in /workspace, so a mount the runtime does not share (macOS file sharing, SELinux labels) is blocked rather than reported as a leak, and dependent probes are skipped (test_an_unusable_workspace_mount_is_blocked_not_unqualified, test_an_unwritable_empty_mount_is_blocked); unqualified is now reserved for observed violations, documented in docs/qualification-suite.md.

evidence: artifact_lineage.py: content identity (SHA-256) is deduplicated while each sighting appends its own ProvenanceEntry (source_kind, source_ref, trust, confidentiality, operation lists, task, security generation); nothing overwrites an entry, so a later trusted sighting cannot launder an earlier untrusted one (AC1)

artifact_lineage.py: effective_trust is the weakest entry, effective_confidentiality the strictest, and check_operation is deny-wins across every entry; unknown content reports untrusted/secret and refuses every operation; a derivation parent that was never seen is a stub, not a trusted origin (AC1)

artifact_lineage.py: invalidate() records a reason, cascades to derived artifacts (bounded depth) and moves evidence over the artifact to stale without deleting bytes or history; record_evidence stores source-file digests plus the security generation, and accept_evidence refuses on source_changed / source_missing / subject_invalidated / security_generation_changed and writes the refusal into the record so it cannot be flipped back to valid (AC2)

workflow_state.py + app.py: _verify_task_completion_impl captures the security configuration generation before gathering evidence and again before returning a verdict, returning failure_code=security_configuration_changed_during_verification when it moved; app.py supplies the provider from SecurityIncidentStore.summary()['current_generation_seq'], and no provider means 'not checked' rather than 'unchanged' (AC2 at the live completion gate)
